Sketch catalogGetting startedAll sketch instructions

Run any of the 30 sketches

Every sketch is a standalone program you can upload with free Arduino tools. No AI subscription is needed. Begin with setup and your first upload, then use these instructions for your next project.

All sketches start without external components. Sensor and signal projects include optional wiring guidance. The four games play themselves with local decision code.

The repository records compilation with UNO Q core 0.56.0 on the original board. Typed serial input and most visual behavior still need hardware verification. These instructions describe the source code, not a new hardware test.

matrix-light-show

Start here · Read source

What you should see

Eight blue animations rotate automatically, with transitions between effects. No commands are needed.

What you need

No external components; uses the built-in LEDs or matrix.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open matrix-light-show/matrix-light-show.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash matrix-light-show

For a check without uploading: python3 flash matrix-light-show --compile-only.

Try it

Watch a full cycle and identify the rain, scanner, and comet patterns.

This sketch has no serial command controls. Change its source and upload again to customize it.

matrix-marquee

Serial commands · Read source

What you should see

HELLO FROM UNO Q scrolls repeatedly at startup.

What you need

No external components; uses the built-in LEDs or matrix.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge and ArduinoGraphics. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open matrix-marquee/matrix-marquee.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash matrix-marquee

For a check without uploading: python3 flash matrix-marquee --compile-only.

Try it

Send TEXT HELLO SAM, then SPEED 40. The next completed scroll should use your new message and speed.

Send commands

Use the serial monitor at 115200 baud with newline endings, one command per line. Replace bracketed values; a slash separates alternatives.

  • TEXT <message> — set the repeating message, up to 120 characters
  • ONCE <message> — scroll once, then return to the repeating message
  • SPEED <ms> — 20–500 milliseconds per step; lower is faster
  • CLEAR — clear the repeating message
  • HELP — list commands

Serial input still needs end-to-end verification. Settings reset when the sketch restarts.

Limits and tips

Commands take effect only between scroll passes. A long message at a slow speed can take minutes; test with short messages. The repeating message survives between scrolls, not across sketch restarts.

matrix-display-server

Serial commands · Read source

What you should see

A single dim pixel appears at the bottom-right until you send a command.

What you need

No external components; uses the built-in LEDs or matrix.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge and ArduinoGraphics. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open matrix-display-server/matrix-display-server.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash matrix-display-server

For a check without uploading: python3 flash matrix-display-server --compile-only.

Try it

Send BAR 75. Expect an OK reply and a mostly filled horizontal bar. Then send PIX 6 0 7 to light a top-center pixel.

Send commands

Use the serial monitor at 115200 baud with newline endings, one command per line. Replace bracketed values; a slash separates alternatives.

  • TEXT <message> — scroll once, then restore the frame
  • BAR <0-100> — horizontal progress bar
  • METER <0-100> <0-100> — two vertical meters
  • ROW <y> <13 digits 0-7> — replace one row, y = 0–7
  • PIX <x> <y> <0-7> — set a pixel, x = 0–12 and y = 0–7
  • FILL <0-7> — fill the frame
  • BLINK <1-10> — blink the current frame
  • CLEAR — turn all pixels off
  • HELP — list commands

Serial input still needs end-to-end verification. Settings reset when the sketch restarts.

Limits and tips

TEXT replies after scrolling finishes. Pixel coordinates start at the top-left (0, 0). Wait for each reply before sending the next command.

pomodoro-timer

Serial commands · Read source

What you should see

A 25-minute work phase starts immediately. The matrix slowly drains; breaks last 5 minutes, with a 15-minute break after four work phases.

What you need

No external components; uses the built-in LEDs or matrix.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open pomodoro-timer/pomodoro-timer.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash pomodoro-timer

For a check without uploading: python3 flash pomodoro-timer --compile-only.

Try it

Send WORK 1 and RESET for a short trial, then STATUS. PAUSE freezes the timer and RESUME continues it.

Send commands

Use the serial monitor at 115200 baud with newline endings, one command per line. Replace bracketed values; a slash separates alternatives.

  • START / RESUME — start or resume
  • PAUSE — freeze remaining time
  • SKIP — advance to the next phase
  • RESET — restart the work cycle and clear the tally
  • WORK <minutes> / BREAK <minutes> / LONG <minutes> — durations, clamped to 1–120
  • STATUS — report phase and remaining time

Serial input still needs end-to-end verification. Settings reset when the sketch restarts.

analog-csv-logger

Sensors / serial · Read source

What you should see

A0, A1, and A2 stream raw readings at 2 samples per second; the matrix shows bars. Unconnected pins produce noise.

What you need

No components needed for a noise demo. For real data, connect a 0–3.3 V signal to A0–A5 and share GND; see the optional potentiometer example in the setup guide.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open analog-csv-logger/analog-csv-logger.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash analog-csv-logger

For a check without uploading: python3 flash analog-csv-logger --compile-only.

Try it

Send CH A0, RATE 5, and HEADER on separate lines. Expect a timestamp and A0 value in each data row.

Send commands

Use the serial monitor at 115200 baud with newline endings, one command per line. Replace bracketed values; a slash separates alternatives.

  • START / STOP — start or pause logging
  • RATE <0.2-200> — samples per second
  • CH <mask or list> — CH 111000 enables A0–A2; CH A0,A3 selects A0 and A3
  • RAW / VOLTS — raw counts or a voltage estimate
  • HEADER — print column names
  • STATUS — report settings

Serial input still needs end-to-end verification. Settings reset when the sketch restarts.

Limits and tips

VOLTS assumes 10-bit readings (0–1023) and a 3.3 V reference in this code; it is an estimate, not a calibrated measurement. For a recording, run the network monitor from the setup guide with | tee data.csv appended in a Linux/macOS shell. Monitor banners and # comment lines may need removal before importing the numeric rows. Do not assume the CSV format is accepted directly by every Serial Plotter version.

Send commands

Use the serial monitor at 115200 baud with newline endings, one command per line. Replace bracketed values; a slash separates alternatives.

  • COIN — heads or tails

Serial input still needs end-to-end verification. Settings reset when the sketch restarts.

square-wave-generator

Signals / serial · Read source

What you should see

Channel 1 drives D13 at 1 Hz and 50% duty immediately; the built-in LED mirrors it. The upper matrix half shows its waveform.

What you need

Disconnect attached circuits before uploading: D13 is driven at startup. No components are needed to see the built-in LED demo. For measurements, use a compatible oscilloscope or logic analyzer with common GND. Never connect an output to another output.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open square-wave-generator/square-wave-generator.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash square-wave-generator

For a check without uploading: python3 flash square-wave-generator --compile-only.

Try it

With external circuits disconnected, send OUT 1 D9 2 50, then STATUS. Channel 1 moves to D9 at 2 Hz. Send OFF 1 to drive it LOW.

Send commands

Use the serial monitor at 115200 baud with newline endings, one command per line. Replace bracketed values; a slash separates alternatives.

  • OUT <1|2> <D2-D13> <0.1-1000> <1-99> — channel, pin, frequency in Hz, duty in percent
  • OFF <1|2> — stop the channel and drive its pin LOW
  • SWEEP <channel> <start Hz> <end Hz> <seconds> — logarithmic sweep; 0.1–1000 Hz and 0.1–3600 seconds; configure OUT first
  • STATUS — report both channels
  • HELP — list commands

Serial input still needs end-to-end verification. Settings reset when the sketch restarts.

Limits and tips

This uses software timing, not a precision hardware signal source. High frequencies and extreme duty cycles can have substantial jitter. The matrix samples slowly and cannot show a high-frequency waveform accurately.

rtc-matrix-clock

Intermediate · Read source

What you should see

A binary-coded clock displays hours, minutes, and seconds. The monitor prints the full date and time once a second.

What you need

No external components; uses the built-in LEDs or matrix.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open rtc-matrix-clock/rtc-matrix-clock.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash rtc-matrix-clock

For a check without uploading: python3 flash rtc-matrix-clock --compile-only.

Try it

Read columns 1/2 for hours, 5/6 for minutes, and 9/10 for seconds (columns start at 0). From row 7 upward, bright bits are worth 1, 2, 4, and 8. Add them for each digit; ignore the dim baseline markers.

This sketch has no serial command controls. Change its source and upload again to customize it.

Limits and tips

When the RTC is not running, the sketch seeds it from compile time. An already running RTC is left alone. This is not internet time synchronization and has no serial SET command; rebuilding alone does not necessarily reset the clock.

i2c-scanner

Sensors · Read source

What you should see

The serial monitor lists addresses on the SDA/SCL header bus every five seconds. With no devices, an empty scan is expected. The matrix is not used.

What you need

No components needed for an empty scan. Optional: a compatible I2C device on the SDA/SCL header pins with common GND and its required supply. Power down before wiring. Qwiic uses a separate bus; read the limitation below.

Library Manager: Arduino_RouterBridge. Board-specific headers come with the UNO Q core.

Upload

Complete setup once. In Arduino IDE, open i2c-scanner/i2c-scanner.ino, select Arduino UNO Q and its port, then Verify → Upload. Uploading replaces the current sketch.

Or run this from the repository root in the UNO Q Linux terminal, then confirm with y:

python3 flash i2c-scanner

For a check without uploading: python3 flash i2c-scanner --compile-only.

Try it

Try the empty-bus scan first. Then power down, attach a compatible I2C device on the header bus, and compare the next scan after powering up.

This sketch has no serial command controls. Change its source and upload again to customize it.

Limits and tips

This sketch calls Wire.begin(), Wire.beginTransmission(), and Wire.endTransmission(). Current Arduino documentation assigns the Qwiic connector to Wire1. For a Qwiic experiment, replace those three Wire calls with Wire1, then Verify and Upload; that variant has not been compiled or hardware-tested here. The original header comment describing Qwiic scanning is too broad. Device-name annotations are guesses based on addresses, not positive identification.
